## 7. Max-plus optimisation: residuation and the principal solution

### 7.1 Setup

**Definition 7.1.** For $A \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}$ and $x \in \mathbb{R}^n$
define the max-plus matrix–vector product
$$(A \otimes x)_i \;=\; \max_{1 \le j \le n} \bigl(A_{ij} + x_j\bigr),$$
and for $b \in \mathbb{R}^m$ the *residuated vector*
$$(A \,\sharp\, b)_j \;=\; \min_{1 \le i \le m} \bigl(b_i - A_{ij}\bigr).$$

Interpretation: $A_{ij}$ is the delay from event $j$ to event $i$, $x_j$ the
occurrence time of $j$, $b_i$ the deadline for $i$; then $(A\sharp b)_j$ is the
latest time $j$ may occur without violating any deadline.

### 7.2 The Galois connection

**Theorem 7.2 (Residuation).** *For all $x \in \mathbb{R}^n$,*
$$A \otimes x \le b \iff x \le A \,\sharp\, b$$
*(both inequalities coordinatewise). In particular $A \sharp b$ is the greatest
subsolution of $A \otimes x \le b$, and it is always a subsolution.*

*Proof.* ($\Rightarrow$) Fix $j$. For every $i$, $A_{ij} + x_j \le (A\otimes x)_i
\le b_i$, so $x_j \le b_i - A_{ij}$; taking the minimum over $i$ gives
$x_j \le (A\sharp b)_j$.

($\Leftarrow$) Fix $i$. For every $j$, $x_j \le (A\sharp b)_j \le b_i - A_{ij}$,
so $A_{ij} + x_j \le b_i$; taking the maximum over $j$ gives $(A \otimes x)_i \le
b_i$. Applying this with $x = A\sharp b$ shows $A \sharp b$ is a subsolution.
$\square$

**Lemma 7.3 (Monotonicity).** *If $x \le y$ coordinatewise then
$A \otimes x \le A \otimes y$.* Immediate from monotonicity of $\max$ and $+$.

### 7.3 The principal solution

**Theorem 7.4 (Cuninghame-Green principal solution criterion).** *The system
$A \otimes x = b$ has a solution if and only if $A \otimes (A \sharp b) = b$.*

*Proof.* ($\Leftarrow$) Trivial: $A \sharp b$ is then a solution.

($\Rightarrow$) Let $x$ satisfy $A \otimes x = b$. Then $A \otimes x \le b$, so
$x \le A \sharp b$ by Theorem 7.2. By Lemma 7.3,
$$b \;=\; A \otimes x \;\le\; A \otimes (A \sharp b) \;\le\; b,$$
the last inequality because $A\sharp b$ is a subsolution. Hence equality.
$\square$

**Corollary 7.5 (Decision procedure).** *Solvability of a max-plus linear system
$A \otimes x = b$ with $A \in \mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$ is decidable in $O(mn)$
arithmetic operations: compute $A \sharp b$ ($mn$ subtractions and comparisons),
compute $A \otimes (A \sharp b)$ ($mn$ additions and comparisons), and test
equality with $b$ ($m$ comparisons). When solvable, $A \sharp b$ is the greatest
solution.*

This is the max-plus analogue of Gaussian elimination — with the pleasant
difference that there is nothing to eliminate: the candidate solution is a closed
formula, and the only question is whether it works.

**Proposition 7.6 (Monotone defect).** *If $b \le c$ coordinatewise then
$A \otimes (A \sharp b) \le A \otimes (A \sharp c)$; i.e. the best max-plus
approximation of a target from below is monotone in the target.*

*Proof.* $b \le c$ gives $(A\sharp b)_j = \min_i (b_i - A_{ij}) \le \min_i (c_i -
A_{ij}) = (A\sharp c)_j$; apply Lemma 7.3. $\square$

## 8. Consequences for feasibility, and the boundary of the theory

### 8.1 Locality of tropical linear feasibility

**Definition.** For $a,b \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, the *two-sided tropical halfspace*
in $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ is
$$H(a,b) \;=\; \Bigl\{x : \max_j (a_j + x_j) \le \max_j (b_j + x_j)\Bigr\}.$$

Each $H(a,b)$ is a tropical cone: if $x, y \in H(a,b)$ and
$z_i = \max(s+x_i,t+y_i)$, then
$\max_j (c_j + z_j) = \max\bigl(s + \max_j(c_j+x_j),\, t + \max_j(c_j+y_j)\bigr)$
for any vector $c$, since $\max$ distributes over $\max$ and $+$; applying this
identity to $c = a$ and $c = b$ and using $\max(\alpha,\beta) \le
\max(\alpha',\beta')$ whenever $\alpha \le \alpha'$, $\beta \le \beta'$ gives
$z \in H(a,b)$.

**Theorem 8.1 (Tropical linear feasibility is $(d+1)$-local).** *A finite system
of two-sided tropical linear inequalities in $d+1$ unknowns,*
$$\max_j \bigl(a_{kj}+x_j\bigr) \;\le\; \max_j \bigl(b_{kj}+x_j\bigr), \qquad
k = 1,\dots,n,$$
*is solvable if and only if every subsystem of at most $d+1$ of the inequalities
is solvable.*

*Proof.* Apply Theorem 3.3 in dimension $d+1$ to the cones $H(a_k, b_k)$.
$\square$

Consequently, infeasibility of a tropical linear system in $N$ unknowns always
has a certificate of size $N$: a subsystem of $N$ inequalities that is already
infeasible. This is the max-plus analogue of the Helly-type locality principle
for linear programming.

### 8.2 Difference constraints and Bellman–Ford

**Definition.** For $i,j \in \{1,\dots,d\}$ and $w \in \mathbb{R}$ let
$D(i,j,w) = \{x \in \mathbb{R}^d : x_j \le w + x_i\}$. This is a tropical cone
(check: if $x_j \le w + x_i$ and $y_j \le w + y_i$, then
$\max(s+x_j, t+y_j) \le w + \max(s+x_i, t+y_i)$).

**Theorem 8.3 (Helly criterion for difference constraints).** *Let $d \ge 1$. A
finite system of difference constraints $x_{t_k} - x_{s_k} \le w_k$
($k=1,\dots,n$) in $d$ variables is feasible if and only if every $d$ of the
constraints are simultaneously feasible.*

*Proof.* Apply Theorem 3.3 to the cones $D(s_k,t_k,w_k)$. $\square$

**Remark 8.4 (Agreement with the negative-cycle criterion).** Difference
constraint systems are exactly single-source shortest-path problems: feasibility
holds iff the digraph on $\{1,\dots,d\}$ with an arc $s_k \to t_k$ of weight
$w_k$ has no negative cycle. A negative cycle can be taken simple, hence uses at
most $d$ arcs, i.e. at most $d$ constraints. Theorem 8.3 reproves this bound
without any graph theory: the Helly number of tropical cones and the length of a
simple cycle are the same $d$, and this is not a coincidence — both express that
max-plus dependence in $\mathbb{R}^d$ occurs already among $d$ objects. The
Bellman–Ford algorithm, which detects a negative cycle in $O(dn)$ time, is thus
an efficient realisation of the Helly certificate in this special case.

### 8.3 Finiteness is essential

**Theorem 8.5 (Failure for infinite families).** *There is a countable family of
tropical cones in $\mathbb{R}^2$ such that every finite subfamily has a common
point but the whole family does not.*

*Proof.* Let $C_k = \{x \in \mathbb{R}^2 : x_1 + k \le x_2\}$ for $k \in
\mathbb{N}$; each is a tropical cone (it is $D(1,2,\cdot)$ up to renaming, or
check directly as in §8.2). Given a finite $F \subseteq \mathbb{N}$, the point
$x = (0, \max F)$ lies in $\bigcap_{k \in F} C_k$. But a point in all $C_k$ would
satisfy $x_2 - x_1 \ge k$ for every $k \in \mathbb{N}$, impossible. $\square$

Classically one restores Helly for infinite families by assuming compactness.
Tropical cones are never compact — they are invariant under the unbounded scaling
action of Lemma 3.1 — so no such repair is available in this setting. Any
infinite-family version of tropical Helly must be phrased on the projective torus
with an additional closedness/boundedness assumption there.

## 9. Algorithms

We record the three algorithms implicit in the proofs.

**Algorithm A (Cramer weights and dependence certificate).**
Input $A \in \mathbb{R}^{(d+1)\times d}$. For each $k$, compute
$\lambda_k = \operatorname{tropdet} A^{(\hat k)}$ by solving a $d\times d$
optimal assignment problem. Output $\lambda$ together with, for each coordinate
$i$, the (at least two) maximisers of $\lambda_k + A_{ki}$. Complexity: $O(d^4)$
with the Hungarian algorithm, $O(d \cdot d! \cdot d)$ by brute force.
Correctness: Theorem 2.4.

**Algorithm B (Helly witness / tropical intersection point).** Input: an oracle
producing, for each index $k$, a point $y_k$ in all cones but possibly $C_k$.
Select $d+1$ indices, compute Cramer weights $\lambda$ of the matrix of the
$y_k$, and output $z_i = \max_r (\lambda_r + y_{k_r,i})$. Correctness: the proof
of Theorem 3.3. Recursively unfolding the induction gives a witness for a family
of $n$ cones from $d$-wise witnesses.

**Algorithm C (Principal solution / solvability test).** Input
$A \in \mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$, $b \in \mathbb{R}^m$. Compute
$\hat x_j = \min_i (b_i - A_{ij})$, then $r_i = \max_j (A_{ij} + \hat x_j)$;
report "solvable with greatest solution $\hat x$" if $r = b$, else "unsolvable".
Complexity $O(mn)$. Correctness: Theorem 7.4.

**Algorithm D (Carathéodory reduction).** Input generators $p_k$, $k \in F$, and
weights $\lambda$. For each coordinate $i$ record an argmax $\kappa(i)$; output
$G = \{\kappa(1),\dots,\kappa(d)\}$ and the restricted weights. Complexity
$O(d|F|)$. Correctness: Theorem 5.1.

## 10. Applications

**Scheduling and timetables.** Max-plus linear systems $A \otimes x = b$ model
synchronisation: task $i$ starts when all its predecessors $j$ have finished,
$A_{ij}$ being the transfer delay. Corollary 7.5 gives a linear-time answer to
"can the timetable be met exactly?", together with the latest feasible schedule
$A\sharp b$ when the answer is yes, and the best achievable schedule from below
when it is not (Proposition 7.6).

**Infeasibility certificates.** Theorems 8.1 and 8.3 say that infeasible
max-plus systems fail *locally*: there is always a subsystem of size at most the
number of variables that is itself infeasible. This is the structural reason
tropical feasibility admits short refutations, and matches the negative-cycle
certificates familiar from shortest-path algorithms.

**Generator reduction.** Theorem 5.1 shows any point of a tropical cone hull is a
combination of at most $d$ generators, so a redundant generating set can be
pruned pointwise to $d$ elements in $O(d|F|)$ time — useful whenever tropical
polytopes are computed and stored (tropical polytope algorithms, min-plus matrix
factorisation, and piecewise-linear function representation).

**Piecewise-linear function theory.** A max-plus combination
$z_i = \max_k (\lambda_k + p_{ki})$ is precisely a convex piecewise-linear
function of the weights; the Carathéodory bound says the "effective support" of
such a representation in $d$ coordinates is at most $d$, a statement of interest
in the study of ReLU networks, where max-plus hull dimension controls
expressivity.

---

## 11. Discussion

Two themes run through the results.

**Coordinates, not dimensions.** Classical convexity numbers count dimensions:
Carathéodory $d+1$, Helly $d+1$, Radon $d+2$, all inherited from the $d+1$
vertices of a $d$-simplex. Tropical convexity counts *coordinates*: Carathéodory
$d$, Helly $d$, because a max-plus combination is decided coordinatewise, one
witness per coordinate. Theorem 5.1 makes this explicit — its proof is literally
"choose one generator per coordinate". Theorem 3.3 is the same idea run through
Cramer dependence; and Theorem 4.3, where scaling invariance is absent, pays back
exactly the one unit that the homogenisation coordinate costs.

**Ties replace cancellation.** In the absence of additive inverses, the algebraic
notion of "$\sum c_k v_k = 0$" is replaced by "the maximum is attained twice".
Theorem 2.4 shows the classical determinantal machinery survives this
replacement essentially verbatim: the identity "two equal columns $\Rightarrow$
singular" becomes "two equal columns $\Rightarrow$ two optimal assignments", and
the swap of columns becomes the swap of the rows carrying them. Everything else
in the paper — the Helly theorem, its converse, the residuation argument — is
downstream of this single tie.

**Sharpness everywhere.** All three constants ($d$ for cone Helly, $d+1$ for
convex Helly, $d$ for cone Carathéodory) come with explicit extremal families,
and they are strikingly simple: "some other coordinate beats coordinate $k$ by
$1$" for Helly, the tropical unit vectors for Carathéodory. That the extremal
objects are this rigid suggests that the constants are structural rather than
accidental.

---

## 12. Future Directions

**Conjecture 12.1 (Tropical Radon number is $d+1$).** *Any $d+1$ points of
$\mathbb{R}^d$ can be split into two nonempty groups whose tropical cone hulls
intersect.*

The key insight is that a Radon partition is exactly a proper 2-colouring of the
*argmax hypergraph* $\{M_i\}$ of a dependence witness $\lambda$ (edge $M_i$ = set
of rows attaining the maximum in coordinate $i$): the partition works iff every
$M_i$ is bichromatic. The Cramer witness of Theorem 2.4 already forces
$|M_i| \ge 2$, but a hypergraph with $d$ edges of size $\ge 2$ on $d+1$ vertices
can fail property B (a triangle plus isolated vertices), so the conjecture needs
an *optimisation over the whole dependence polytope*
$$\Lambda = \{\lambda : \text{every column maximum is attained twice}\}$$
rather than one point of it. Why now? $\Lambda$ is a nonempty polyhedral complex
by Theorem 2.4, so the question is a concrete finite optimisation over an
explicitly constructed object, and Levi's inequality (Helly $\le$ Radon $-1$) is
already tight at $d$ on the extremal family of Definition 3.5, which is exactly
what a Radon number $d+1$ predicts.

**Conjecture 12.2 (Colourful tropical Helly).** Let $F_1,\dots,F_d$ be finite
families ("colours") of tropical cones in $\mathbb{R}^d$. If every rainbow
selection (one cone from each colour) has a common point, then some single colour
class has a common point. The colourful Carathéodory theorem (Theorem 5.4)
supplies exactly the kind of rainbow selection mechanism such a proof needs.

**Further directions.**

- *Fractional and $(p,q)$ versions.* Fractional Helly theorems and Alon–Kleitman
  $(p,q)$-theorems for tropical cones, with the constant $d$ in place of $d+1$.
- *Infinite families on the torus.* Identify the correct compactness hypothesis
  on $\mathbb{R}^d/\mathbb{R}\mathbf{1}$ under which Theorem 3.3 extends to
  infinite families, repairing Theorem 8.5.
- *Signed and symmetrised tropical settings.* Extend the Cramer dependence
  theorem to the symmetrised max-plus semiring, where a genuine notion of
  "balanced" replaces "attained twice", and ask whether the Helly number changes.
- *Algorithmic Helly.* Turn Algorithm B into a practical algorithm computing a
  point in the intersection of $n$ tropical cones given only $d$-wise oracles,
  and analyse its complexity as a function of $n$ and $d$.
- *Boundary cases with $-\infty$.* All results here are stated over the finite
  part $\mathbb{R}$; allowing $-\infty$ entries (genuinely partial max-plus
  vectors) changes the geometry of the extremal families and the constants
  deserve to be re-examined.

\begin{abstract}
We develop the combinatorial convexity of the max-plus semiring
$(\R,\oplus,\odot)=(\R,\max,+)$ and determine exactly the two fundamental
invariants of tropical convexity in $\R^d$. We prove a \emph{tropical Cramer
dependence theorem}: any $d+1$ vectors of $\R^d$ are tropically dependent, with
explicit witnessing weights given by the tropical determinants of the
row-deleted minors. From it we deduce a \emph{tropical Helly theorem with Helly
number exactly $d$} for tropical cones (max-plus submodules) in $\R^d$ --- one
better than the classical bound $d+1$ --- together with a matching extremal
family. For the weaker notion of tropically convex sets (no scaling invariance)
we prove the Helly number is exactly $d+1$, again with a matching extremal
family; this settles in the affirmative, with a strictly better constant, a
previously conjectured bound of $2d$, and shows that the conjecture as stated
fails in the degenerate case $d=0$. We show the implication is reversible: the
Helly property, taken as a hypothesis, forces tropical dependence, so the Helly
theorem and the Cramer dependence theorem are equivalent. On the Carath\'eodory
side we prove that the \emph{Carath\'eodory number of tropical cone hulls in
$\R^d$ is exactly $d$}, and establish a constructive \emph{colourful
Carath\'eodory theorem}. Finally we connect the geometry to max-plus
optimisation: we prove the \emph{residuation (Galois) correspondence}
$A\otimes x\le b \iff x\le A\sharp b$ and the \emph{principal-solution
solvability criterion}, giving an $O(mn)$ decision procedure for
$A\otimes x=b$; and we derive from Helly that tropical linear feasibility is
$(d+1)$-local and difference-constraint feasibility is $d$-local --- the
Helly-theoretic shadow of the Bellman--Ford negative-cycle criterion. We also
show finiteness is essential: Helly fails for infinite families of tropical

\section{Introduction}

\subsection{The max-plus semiring}

Let $\R_{\max}=(\R\cup\{-\infty\},\oplus,\odot)$ with $a\oplus b=\max(a,b)$ and
$a\odot b=a+b$. Throughout we work over the \emph{finite} part $\R$: all
statements concern vectors in $\R^d$ with real entries and real weights, the
setting in which the tropical projective torus $\R^d/\R\mathbf 1$ is a genuine
manifold and the sharp constants below are attained.

The semiring $\R_{\max}$ is the arithmetic of a large family of discrete
optimisation problems: shortest paths, critical-path scheduling, dynamic
programming, Viterbi decoding, and the tropicalisation of algebraic varieties
are all instances of max-plus (or the isomorphic min-plus) linear algebra. It is
therefore natural to ask which structural theorems of classical convex geometry
survive the change of arithmetic, and with which constants.

\subsection{Tropical convexity}

\begin{definition}[Tropical cone]
A set $S\subseteq\R^d$ is a \emph{tropical cone} (a max-plus submodule) if for
all $x,y\in S$ and all $s,t\in\R$,
\[ \bigl(i\mapsto \max(s+x_i,\;t+y_i)\bigr)\in S. \]
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Tropically convex set]
A set $S\subseteq\R^d$ is \emph{tropically convex} if for all $x,y\in S$ and all
$t\le 0$,
\[ \bigl(i\mapsto \max(x_i,\;t+y_i)\bigr)\in S. \]
\end{definition}

The second definition is the normalised version: the weights $0$ and $t\le 0$
are the max-plus analogue of coefficients summing to the tropical unit. Every
tropical cone is tropically convex; conversely a tropically convex set need not
be closed under tropical scaling $x\mapsto s\odot x=(s+x_1,\dots,s+x_d)$. Taking
$x=y$ and $s=t$ in the first definition shows tropical cones \emph{are} scaling
invariant, so they descend to the tropical projective torus. This single fact is
the source of the one-unit gap between the two Helly numbers below.

\begin{definition}[Tropical cone hull]
For a family $(p_k)_{k\in\iota}$ in $\R^d$ and a nonempty finite $F\subseteq
\iota$,
\[ \tcone(p;F)=\Bigl\{z\in\R^d:\ \exists\,\lambda\in\R^{\iota},\ \forall i,\
z_i=\max_{k\in F}(\lambda_k+p_{ki})\Bigr\}. \]
It is the smallest tropical cone containing $\{p_k : k\in F\}$.
\end{definition}

\section{Tropical Cramer dependence}

\begin{definition}[Tropical determinant]
For $M\in\R^{m\times m}$,
\[ \tropdet M \;=\; \max_{\pi\in\Sym_m}\ \sum_{r=1}^{m} M_{r,\pi(r)} . \]
\end{definition}

This is the value of the optimal assignment problem with cost matrix $M$; it is
the max-plus permanent, which coincides with the determinant because there are
no signs. Crucially, $\tropdet$ is a maximum over $m!$ terms, and \emph{ties}
between optimal permutations are the tropical replacement for a vanishing
determinant.

\begin{definition}[Tropical dependence]
Vectors $A_0,\dots,A_d\in\R^d$ (rows of $A\in\R^{(d+1)\times d}$) are
\emph{tropically dependent} if there are weights $\lambda\in\R^{d+1}$ such that
for every coordinate $i$ the maximum $\max_k(\lambda_k+A_{ki})$ is attained by
at least two distinct indices $k$.
\end{definition}

Equivalently: for every coordinate $i$ and every index $k$ there is $j\ne k$
with $\lambda_k+A_{ki}\le\lambda_j+A_{ji}$.

\begin{definition}[Cramer weight]
For $A\in\R^{(d+1)\times d}$ and $0\le k\le d$ let $A^{(\hat k)}\in\R^{d\times
d}$ be $A$ with row $k$ deleted, and put $\lambda_k=\tropdet A^{(\hat k)}$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Tropical Cramer dependence]\label{thm:cramer}
For every $A\in\R^{(d+1)\times d}$ and every coordinate $i$, the maximum
$\max_k(\lambda_k+A_{ki})$ over the Cramer weights is attained at (at least) two
distinct rows. Consequently any $d+1$ vectors of $\R^d$ are tropically
dependent, with explicitly computable witnessing weights.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Fix $i$ and form the augmented square matrix $\widetilde A^{(i)}\in
\R^{(d+1)\times(d+1)}$ obtained from $A$ by prepending a copy of its own $i$-th
column; thus columns $0$ and $i+1$ of $\widetilde A^{(i)}$ are equal.

\emph{Step 1 (Laplace expansion).} For $\pi\in\Sym_{d+1}$ let
$W(\pi)=\sum_r\widetilde A^{(i)}_{r,\pi(r)}$ and $k=\pi^{-1}(0)$. Deleting row
$k$ and column $0$ turns $\pi$ into a bijection of the remaining rows onto the
original columns, so
\[ W(\pi)=A_{ki}+\sum_{r\ne k}A_{r,\pi(r)-1}\le A_{ki}+\tropdet A^{(\hat k)}
=\lambda_k+A_{ki}, \]
with equality attained by extending an optimal permutation of $A^{(\hat k)}$ by
$k\mapsto 0$. Hence $\tropdet\widetilde A^{(i)}=\max_k(\lambda_k+A_{ki})$.

\emph{Step 2 (two equal columns).} Let $\pi$ be optimal, $a=\pi^{-1}(0)$,
$b=\pi^{-1}(i+1)$; then $a\ne b$. Since columns $0$ and $i+1$ are equal, the
swapped permutation $\pi'=\pi\circ(a\,b)$ has $W(\pi')=W(\pi)$, so $\pi'$ is
also optimal.

\emph{Step 3.} Step 1 applied to $\pi$ gives $\tropdet\widetilde
A^{(i)}=\lambda_a+A_{ai}$; applied to $\pi'$, whose row receiving column $0$ is
$b$, it gives $\lambda_b+A_{bi}$. As $a\ne b$, the maximum is attained twice.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
The proof is the max-plus incarnation of ``a matrix with two equal columns is
singular''. Classically one swaps the equal columns to see that the determinant
equals its own negative; tropically, where there are no signs, one swaps the two
\emph{rows carrying} the equal columns to see that the optimal assignment is not
unique. Non-uniqueness of the optimum is the tropical form of vanishing.
\end{remark}

\begin{remark}[Complexity and sharpness]
The Cramer weights are $d+1$ optimal assignment values on $d\times d$ matrices,
computable in $O(d^4)$ total time by the Hungarian algorithm. The number $d+1$
of vectors cannot be lowered: for $A=\begin{psmallmatrix}0&0\\1&3
\end{psmallmatrix}$ a dependence would need both $\lambda_0=\lambda_1+1$ and
$\lambda_0=\lambda_1+3$.
\end{remark}

\section{The tropical Helly theorem for cones}

\begin{lemma}[Scaling invariance]\label{lem:shift}
If $S$ is a tropical cone and $x\in S$ then $(s+x_i)_i\in S$ for all $s\in\R$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Take $y=x$, $t=s$ in the definition.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Finite combinations]\label{lem:sup}
If $S$ is a tropical cone, $F$ finite nonempty, $p_k\in S$ for $k\in F$, and
$\lambda\in\R^F$, then $\bigl(i\mapsto\max_{k\in F}(\lambda_k+p_{ki})\bigr)\in
S$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Induction on $|F|$, the base case being Lemma~\ref{lem:shift} and the inductive
step the defining closure property with $t=0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Tropical Helly theorem, Helly number $d$]\label{thm:helly}
Let $d\ge1$, let $(C_k)_{k\in\iota}$ be tropical cones in $\R^d$ and $F$ a
finite index set. If $\bigcap_{k\in I}C_k\ne\varnothing$ for every $I\subseteq
F$ with $|I|\le d$, then $\bigcap_{k\in F}C_k\ne\varnothing$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Induct on $|F|$. For $|F|\le d$ the claim is the hypothesis. Let $|F|>d$. For
each $k\in F$ the induction hypothesis applied to $F\setminus\{k\}$ yields
$y_k\in\bigcap_{j\in F\setminus\{k\}}C_j$. Choose distinct
$k_0,\dots,k_d\in F$, let $A$ be the matrix with rows $y_{k_0},\dots,y_{k_d}$,
let $\lambda$ be its Cramer weights, and set
$z_i=\max_r(\lambda_r+A_{ri})$.

If $j\notin\{k_0,\dots,k_d\}$, all rows lie in $C_j$ and $z\in C_j$ by
Lemma~\ref{lem:sup}. If $j=k_{r_0}$, only row $r_0$ may fail to lie in $C_j$;
but by Theorem~\ref{thm:cramer} the maximum in each coordinate is attained
twice, hence by some $r\ne r_0$, so $z_i=\max_{r\ne r_0}(\lambda_r+A_{ri})$ for
all $i$ and Lemma~\ref{lem:sup} again gives $z\in C_j$. Thus $z\in\bigcap_{k\in
F}C_k$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}
Under the hypotheses above, $\bigcap_{k\in F}C_k\ne\varnothing$ if and only if
$\bigcap_{k\in I}C_k\ne\varnothing$ for every $I\subseteq F$ with $|I|\le d$:
an empty intersection is always certified by at most $d$ members.
\end{corollary}

\subsection{Sharpness}

\begin{definition}\label{def:tight}
For $1\le k\le d$ put $T_k=\{x\in\R^d:\exists\,j\ne k,\ x_k+1\le x_j\}$.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}
Each $T_k$ is a tropical cone.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Let $x,y\in T_k$ with witnesses $j_x,j_y$, and $z_i=\max(s+x_i,t+y_i)$. If
$s+x_k\ge t+y_k$ then $z_k=s+x_k$ and $z_{j_x}\ge s+x_{j_x}\ge z_k+1$; otherwise
$j_y$ works symmetrically.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:empty}
$\bigcap_{k=1}^{d}T_k=\varnothing$ for $d\ge1$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
If $x$ lies in the intersection, take $k$ maximising $x_k$; the witness $j$ for
$T_k$ gives $x_k+1\le x_j\le x_k$, absurd.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:small}
For every $I\subsetneq\{1,\dots,d\}$, $\bigcap_{k\in I}T_k\ne\varnothing$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Pick $k_0\notin I$ and set $x_{k_0}=0$, $x_j=-1$ for $j\ne k_0$; then $k_0$
witnesses membership in each $T_k$, $k\in I$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Sharpness]
For every $d\ge1$ there are $d$ tropical cones in $\R^d$, any $d-1$ of which
meet, with empty total intersection. With Theorem~\ref{thm:helly}, the tropical
Helly number of $\R^d$ is exactly $d$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{remark}
The gain of one unit over the classical bound $d+1$ is precisely scaling
invariance: a tropical cone is determined by its image in the
$(d-1)$-dimensional torus $\R^d/\R\mathbf1$. The proof above makes this precise
without ever quotienting, via the Cramer weights.
\end{remark}

\section{Helly number $d+1$ for tropically convex sets}

\begin{definition}
Let $\pi:\R^{d+1}\to\R^d$, $\pi(u)_i=u_i-u_{d+1}$, and for $S\subseteq\R^d$ set
$\widehat S=\pi^{-1}(S)\subseteq\R^{d+1}$.
\end{definition}

Since $\pi((x,0))=x$ we have $x\in S\iff(x,0)\in\widehat S$, and $\widehat S$ is
scaling invariant because $\pi(s+u)=\pi(u)$.

\begin{theorem}[Homogenisation]\label{thm:homog}
If $S\subseteq\R^d$ is tropically convex then $\widehat S\subseteq\R^{d+1}$ is a
tropical cone.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Let $u,v\in\widehat S$ and $w_i=\max(s+u_i,t+v_i)$. Using scaling invariance of
$\pi$, normalise $u_{d+1}=v_{d+1}=0$ and $s=0$, so $w=\max(u,t+v)$. If $t\le0$
then $\pi(w)_i=\max(\pi(u)_i,t+\pi(v)_i)\in S$ by tropical convexity; if $t\ge0$
exchange the roles of $u$ and $v$. Hence $w\in\widehat S$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Helly for tropically convex sets]\label{thm:convexhelly}
Let $(S_k)_{k\in\iota}$ be tropically convex subsets of $\R^d$ and $F$ finite.
If every $I\subseteq F$ with $|I|\le d+1$ has $\bigcap_{k\in I}S_k\ne
\varnothing$, then $\bigcap_{k\in F}S_k\ne\varnothing$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The $\widehat{S_k}$ are tropical cones in $\R^{d+1}$ by Theorem~\ref{thm:homog},
and the hypothesis lifts via $x\mapsto(x,0)$. Theorem~\ref{thm:helly} in
dimension $d+1$ gives $u\in\bigcap_k\widehat{S_k}$, and $\pi(u)\in\bigcap_k S_k$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Sharpness]
There exist $d+1$ tropically convex subsets of $\R^d$, any $d$ of which meet,
with empty total intersection; hence the Helly number of tropical convexity in
$\R^d$ is exactly $d+1$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Dehomogenise the family of Definition~\ref{def:tight} one dimension up: for
$1\le k\le d+1$ put $U_k=\{x\in\R^d:(x,0)\in T_k\}$, with $T_k\subseteq
\R^{d+1}$. Tropical convexity of $U_k$ follows because appending $0$ commutes
with the normalised combination when $t\le0$ (as $\max(0,t)=0$). Emptiness is
Lemma~\ref{lem:empty} in dimension $d+1$. For $|I|\le d$, Lemma~\ref{lem:small}
gives $u\in\bigcap_{k\in I}T_k$, and $\pi(u)$ works because $(\pi(u),0)$ is the
tropical scaling of $u$ by $-u_{d+1}$ and tropical cones are scaling invariant.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Resolution of the $2d$ conjecture]
For every $d\ge1$, any finite family of tropically convex subsets of $\R^d$
whose subfamilies of size at most $2d$ intersect has nonempty total
intersection. For $d=0$ the statement is false.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
For $d\ge1$, $d+1\le 2d$, so Theorem~\ref{thm:convexhelly} applies. For $d=0$
the hypothesis is vacuous and $S_1=\varnothing\subseteq\R^0$ is a
counterexample.
\end{proof}

Thus the conjectured constant $2d$ is correct for $d\ge1$ but far from sharp for
$d\ge2$, and $d=0$ must be excluded.

\section{Tropical Carath\'eodory numbers}

\begin{theorem}[Tropical Carath\'eodory for cones]\label{thm:cara}
Let $d\ge1$, $F$ finite, and $z\in\tcone(p;F)$. Then there is $G\subseteq F$
with $|G|\le d$ and $z\in\tcone(p;G)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Write $z_i=\max_{k\in F}(\lambda_k+p_{ki})$ and choose for each coordinate $i$ an
index $\kappa(i)\in F$ attaining the maximum. Put $G=\kappa(\{1,\dots,d\})$, so
$|G|\le d$. With the same weights, $\max_{k\in G}(\lambda_k+p_{ki})\ge
\lambda_{\kappa(i)}+p_{\kappa(i)i}=z_i$, while $\le z_i$ since $G\subseteq F$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Sharpness]
For every $d\ge1$ let $p_{ki}=0$ if $i=k$ and $-1$ otherwise. Then
$\mathbf0\in\tcone(p;\{1,\dots,d\})$, but $\mathbf0\notin\tcone(p;G)$ for every
$G$ with $|G|<d$. The Carath\'eodory number of tropical cones in $\R^d$ is
exactly $d$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
With all weights $0$, $\max_k p_{ki}=p_{ii}=0$. Conversely let $|G|<d$ and
suppose $\mathbf 0=\bigl(\max_{k\in G}(\lambda_k+p_{ki})\bigr)_i$. Choose
$i_0\notin G$. Every $k\in G$ has $p_{ki_0}=-1$, so $0=\max_{k\in
G}(\lambda_k-1)$ and the maximiser $k^\ast$ has $\lambda_{k^\ast}=1$. But then
in coordinate $k^\ast$, $0=\max_{k\in G}(\lambda_k+p_{kk^\ast})\ge
\lambda_{k^\ast}+0=1$, a contradiction.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Colourful tropical Carath\'eodory]\label{thm:colourful}
Let $d\ge1$ and let $p^{(1)},\dots,p^{(d)}$ be families of points of $\R^d$ with
finite nonempty index sets $F_1,\dots,F_d$. If $z\in\tcone(p^{(c)};F_c)$ for
every colour $c$, then there is a rainbow selection $\sigma(c)\in F_c$ and
weights $w\in\R^d$ with
\[ z_i=\max_{1\le c\le d}\bigl(w_c+p^{(c)}_{\sigma(c),i}\bigr),\qquad 1\le i\le
d. \]
Explicitly, from class $c$ take a generator attaining the maximum in coordinate
$c$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Let $\lambda^{(c)}$ realise $z$ in class $c$, let $\sigma(c)$ attain the maximum
in coordinate $i=c$, and put $w_c=\lambda^{(c)}_{\sigma(c)}$. For each $i$ the
colour $c=i$ contributes exactly $z_i$, giving ``$\ge$''; and every term
satisfies $w_c+p^{(c)}_{\sigma(c),i}\le\max_{k\in
F_c}(\lambda^{(c)}_k+p^{(c)}_{ki})=z_i$, giving ``$\le$''.
\end{proof}

The rainbow selection is fully explicit and computable in $O(d\sum_c|F_c|)$
time.

\section{Helly and Cramer are equivalent}

\begin{theorem}[Dependence from Helly]
Let $d\ge1$ and assume: every family of $d+1$ tropical cones in $\R^d$ whose
subfamilies of size $\le d$ intersect has a common point. Then any $d+1$ points
$p_0,\dots,p_d\in\R^d$ are tropically dependent.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Let $H_k=\tcone(p;\{0,\dots,d\}\setminus\{k\})$, a tropical cone by
Lemma~\ref{lem:sup}. Any $d$ of the $H_k$ intersect: if $|I|\le d$, pick
$k_0\notin I$; then $p_{k_0}\in H_k$ for all $k\in I$. By hypothesis there is
$z\in\bigcap_k H_k$. Residuate: $\lambda_j=\min_i(z_i-p_{ji})$, the greatest
weight with $\lambda_j+p_j\le z$. Then (i) $\lambda_j+p_{ji}\le z_i$ for all
$j,i$; and (ii) for every $k$ and $i$, $z_i=\max_{j\ne k}(\lambda_j+p_{ji})$,
because $z\in H_k$ supplies weights $\mu$ with $z_i=\max_{j\ne k}(\mu_j+p_{ji})$
and maximality forces $\mu_j\le\lambda_j$. Fixing $i,k$ and taking $j\ne k$
attaining the maximum in (ii) gives $\lambda_k+p_{ki}\le z_i=\lambda_j+p_{ji}$,
which is tropical dependence.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}
In each dimension $d\ge1$ the tropical Helly theorem and the tropical Cramer
dependence theorem are equivalent.
\end{corollary}

\section{Max-plus optimisation: residuation and the principal solution}

\begin{definition}
For $A\in\R^{m\times n}$, $x\in\R^n$, $b\in\R^m$ set
\[ (A\otimes x)_i=\max_{j}(A_{ij}+x_j),\qquad
(A\,\sharp\,b)_j=\min_i(b_i-A_{ij}). \]
\end{definition}

Interpretation: $A_{ij}$ is the delay from event $j$ to event $i$, $x_j$ the
occurrence time of $j$, $b_i$ the deadline for $i$; then $(A\sharp b)_j$ is the
latest time $j$ may occur without violating a deadline.

\begin{theorem}[Residuation]\label{thm:resid}
For all $x$, $A\otimes x\le b \iff x\le A\,\sharp\,b$ (coordinatewise). In
particular $A\sharp b$ is the greatest subsolution, and is itself a subsolution.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
($\Rightarrow$) For all $i,j$, $A_{ij}+x_j\le(A\otimes x)_i\le b_i$, so
$x_j\le b_i-A_{ij}$; minimise over $i$. ($\Leftarrow$) For all $i,j$,
$x_j\le(A\sharp b)_j\le b_i-A_{ij}$, so $A_{ij}+x_j\le b_i$; maximise over $j$.
Apply with $x=A\sharp b$ for the last claim.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Monotonicity]\label{lem:mono}
If $x\le y$ then $A\otimes x\le A\otimes y$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{theorem}[Principal solution criterion]\label{thm:principal}
$A\otimes x=b$ is solvable if and only if $A\otimes(A\sharp b)=b$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
($\Leftarrow$) Trivial. ($\Rightarrow$) If $A\otimes x=b$ then $x\le A\sharp b$
by Theorem~\ref{thm:resid}, so by Lemma~\ref{lem:mono}
$b=A\otimes x\le A\otimes(A\sharp b)\le b$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}
Solvability of $A\otimes x=b$ is decidable in $O(mn)$ arithmetic operations:
compute $A\sharp b$, then $A\otimes(A\sharp b)$, and compare with $b$. When
solvable, $A\sharp b$ is the greatest solution.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proposition}[Monotone defect]
If $b\le c$ then $A\otimes(A\sharp b)\le A\otimes(A\sharp c)$.
\end{proposition}

\section{Consequences for feasibility, and the boundary of the theory}

\begin{definition}
For $a,b\in\R^{n}$, the two-sided tropical halfspace is
$H(a,b)=\{x:\max_j(a_j+x_j)\le\max_j(b_j+x_j)\}$.
\end{definition}

Each $H(a,b)$ is a tropical cone, because for any $c$ and
$z_i=\max(s+x_i,t+y_i)$ one has
$\max_j(c_j+z_j)=\max\bigl(s+\max_j(c_j+x_j),\,t+\max_j(c_j+y_j)\bigr)$.

\begin{theorem}[Tropical linear feasibility is $(d+1)$-local]
A finite system $\max_j(a_{kj}+x_j)\le\max_j(b_{kj}+x_j)$, $k=1,\dots,n$, in
$d+1$ unknowns is solvable if and only if every subsystem of at most $d+1$
inequalities is solvable.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Helly criterion for difference constraints]
Let $d\ge1$. A finite system $x_{t_k}-x_{s_k}\le w_k$, $k=1,\dots,n$, in $d$
variables is feasible if and only if every $d$ of the constraints are
simultaneously feasible.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The sets $D(i,j,w)=\{x:x_j\le w+x_i\}$ are tropical cones; apply
Theorem~\ref{thm:helly}.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
Difference-constraint systems are exactly shortest-path problems: feasibility
holds iff the associated digraph has no negative cycle, and a negative cycle can
be taken simple, hence with at most $d$ arcs. The Helly bound $d$ reproves this
without graph theory: both numbers express that max-plus dependence in $\R^d$
occurs already among $d$ objects. Bellman--Ford is an efficient realisation of
the Helly certificate in this case.
\end{remark}

\begin{theorem}[Failure for infinite families]
The cones $C_k=\{x\in\R^2: x_1+k\le x_2\}$, $k\in\mathbb N$, are tropical cones,
every finite subfamily has a common point, and the whole family has none.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
For finite $F$ take $x=(0,\max F)$. A point in all $C_k$ would satisfy
$x_2-x_1\ge k$ for every $k$.
\end{proof}

Classically one restores Helly for infinite families using compactness; tropical
cones are never compact, being invariant under the unbounded scaling action, so
finiteness is genuinely essential here.

\section{Algorithms}

\begin{algorithmbox}[Cramer weights and dependence certificate]
Input $A\in\R^{(d+1)\times d}$. For each $k$ compute
$\lambda_k=\tropdet A^{(\hat k)}$ by an optimal assignment solve; output
$\lambda$ and, for each coordinate, the maximisers of $\lambda_k+A_{ki}$.
Complexity $O(d^4)$ with the Hungarian algorithm.
\end{algorithmbox}

\begin{algorithmbox}[Helly witness]
Given points $y_k$ lying in all cones but possibly $C_k$, select $d+1$ indices,
compute the Cramer weights $\lambda$ of the matrix of the $y_k$, and output
$z_i=\max_r(\lambda_r+y_{k_r,i})$.
\end{algorithmbox}

\begin{algorithmbox}[Principal solution]
Compute $\hat x_j=\min_i(b_i-A_{ij})$ and $r=A\otimes\hat x$; report solvable
with greatest solution $\hat x$ iff $r=b$. Complexity $O(mn)$.
\end{algorithmbox}

\begin{algorithmbox}[Carath\'eodory reduction]
For each coordinate $i$ record an argmax $\kappa(i)$ of $\lambda_k+p_{ki}$;
output $G=\{\kappa(1),\dots,\kappa(d)\}$. Complexity $O(d|F|)$.
\end{algorithmbox}

\section{Applications}

\textbf{Scheduling and timetables.} Max-plus systems $A\otimes x=b$ model
synchronisation; the principal-solution criterion answers ``can the timetable be
met exactly?'' in linear time and returns the latest feasible schedule.

\textbf{Infeasibility certificates.} Tropical feasibility fails locally: an
infeasible system always contains an infeasible subsystem of size at most the
number of variables, matching the negative-cycle certificates of shortest-path
algorithms.

\textbf{Generator reduction.} Any point of a tropical cone hull is a combination
of at most $d$ generators, so a redundant generating set can be pruned pointwise
in $O(d|F|)$ time.

\textbf{Piecewise-linear function theory.} A max-plus combination is a convex
piecewise-linear function of the weights; the Carath\'eodory bound says the
effective support of such a representation in $d$ coordinates is at most $d$, a
statement of interest for the expressivity of piecewise-linear (ReLU) networks.

\section{Discussion}

\textbf{Coordinates, not dimensions.} Classical convexity numbers count
dimensions, all inherited from the $d+1$ vertices of a simplex. Tropical
convexity counts \emph{coordinates}: a max-plus combination is decided
coordinatewise, one witness per coordinate. Theorem~\ref{thm:cara} makes this
explicit; Theorem~\ref{thm:helly} runs the same idea through Cramer dependence;
and Theorem~\ref{thm:convexhelly}, where scaling invariance is absent, pays back
exactly the one unit that the homogenising coordinate costs.

\textbf{Ties replace cancellation.} Without additive inverses, ``$\sum c_kv_k=0$''
is replaced by ``the maximum is attained twice''. Theorem~\ref{thm:cramer} shows
the determinantal machinery survives verbatim, and everything else is downstream
of that single tie.

\textbf{Sharpness everywhere.} All three constants come with explicit extremal
families, strikingly simple ones, suggesting the constants are structural rather
than accidental.

\section{Future directions}

\begin{conjecture}[Tropical Radon number is $d+1$]
Any $d+1$ points of $\R^d$ can be split into two nonempty groups whose tropical
cone hulls intersect.
\end{conjecture}

A Radon partition is exactly a proper $2$-colouring of the \emph{argmax
hypergraph} $\{M_i\}$ of a dependence witness $\lambda$ (edge $M_i$ = the set of
rows attaining the maximum in coordinate $i$): the partition works iff every
$M_i$ is bichromatic. The Cramer witness forces $|M_i|\ge2$, but a hypergraph
with $d$ edges of size $\ge2$ on $d+1$ vertices can fail property~B (a triangle
plus isolated vertices), so one needs an optimisation over the whole dependence
polytope $\Lambda=\{\lambda:\text{every column maximum attained twice}\}$ rather
than one point of it. $\Lambda$ is a nonempty polyhedral complex by
Theorem~\ref{thm:cramer}, making this a concrete finite optimisation; and Levi's
inequality (Helly $\le$ Radon $-1$) is already tight at $d$ on the extremal
family of Definition~\ref{def:tight}, exactly as a Radon number $d+1$ predicts.

\begin{conjecture}[Colourful tropical Helly]
Let $F_1,\dots,F_d$ be finite families (``colours'') of tropical cones in $\R^d$.
If every rainbow selection has a common point, then some single colour class has
a common point.
\end{conjecture}

Further directions: fractional and $(p,q)$-type Helly theorems for tropical
cones with the constant $d$; identification of the correct compactness
hypothesis on $\R^d/\R\mathbf1$ under which Helly extends to infinite families;
extension of Cramer dependence to the symmetrised max-plus semiring, where
``balanced'' replaces ``attained twice''; a practical algorithmic version of the
Helly witness construction; and re-examination of all constants when $-\infty$
entries are allowed.

from __future__ import annotations

from itertools import combinations, permutations, product
from typing import Callable, Iterable, Sequence

Vector = list[float]
Matrix = list[list[float]]

NEG_INF = float("-inf")


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Max-plus arithmetic
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def trop_add(a: float, b: float) -> float:
    """Tropical addition a (+) b = max(a, b)."""
    return max(a, b)


def trop_mul(a: float, b: float) -> float:
    """Tropical multiplication a (x) b = a + b."""
    return a + b


def trop_det(M: Matrix) -> float:
    """Tropical determinant  max over permutations pi of  sum_r M[r][pi(r)].

    This is the value of the optimal assignment problem with cost matrix M.
    Brute force over m! permutations; fine for the small m used here.
    """
    m = len(M)
    if m == 0:
        return 0.0
    return max(sum(M[r][pi[r]] for r in range(m)) for pi in permutations(range(m)))


def mul_vec(A: Matrix, x: Vector) -> Vector:
    """Max-plus matrix-vector product  (A (x) x)_i = max_j (A[i][j] + x[j])."""
    return [max(A[i][j] + x[j] for j in range(len(x))) for i in range(len(A))]


def resid(A: Matrix, b: Vector) -> Vector:
    """Residuated vector  (A # b)_j = min_i (b[i] - A[i][j]).

    By the residuation theorem this is the greatest x with A (x) x <= b.
    """
    m, n = len(A), len(A[0])
    return [min(b[i] - A[i][j] for i in range(m)) for j in range(n)]


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Tropical Cramer dependence
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def delete_row(A: Matrix, k: int) -> Matrix:
    """The row-deleted minor A^(k-hat)."""
    return [row[:] for i, row in enumerate(A) if i != k]


def cramer_weights(A: Matrix) -> Vector:
    """Cramer weights lambda_k = tropdet(A with row k deleted).

    A is (d+1) x d.  By the tropical Cramer dependence theorem, for every
    column i the maximum of lambda_k + A[k][i] is attained at >= 2 rows.
    """
    return [trop_det(delete_row(A, k)) for k in range(len(A))]


def column_argmax_profile(A: Matrix, lam: Vector) -> list[tuple[float, int]]:
    """For each column: (value of the max, number of rows attaining it)."""
    out: list[tuple[float, int]] = []
    for i in range(len(A[0])):
        vals = [lam[k] + A[k][i] for k in range(len(A))]
        best = max(vals)
        out.append((best, sum(1 for v in vals if abs(v - best) < 1e-9)))
    return out


def is_tropically_dependent(A: Matrix, lam: Vector) -> bool:
    """Every column maximum of lambda_k + A[k][i] is attained at least twice."""
    return all(cnt >= 2 for _, cnt in column_argmax_profile(A, lam))

# 3. Tropical Helly:  Helly number d for cones

def helly_tight_set(k: int, d: int) -> Callable[[Vector], bool]:
    """Membership test for T_k = {x : exists j != k with x_k + 1 <= x_j}.

    Each T_k is a tropical cone; the family T_1..T_d has empty intersection but
    every d-1 of them meet.  This is the extremal family for Helly number d.
    """

    def member(x: Vector) -> bool:
        return any(j != k and x[k] + 1 <= x[j] + 1e-12 for j in range(d))

    return member


def is_trop_cone_numeric(member: Callable[[Vector], bool], d: int,
                         trials: int = 400) -> bool:
    """Monte-Carlo check that a set is closed under max-plus combinations."""
    import random

    for _ in range(trials):
        x = [float(random.randint(-5, 5)) for _ in range(d)]
        y = [float(random.randint(-5, 5)) for _ in range(d)]
        if not (member(x) and member(y)):
            continue
        s, t = float(random.randint(-4, 4)), float(random.randint(-4, 4))
        z = [max(s + x[i], t + y[i]) for i in range(d)]
        if not member(z):
            return False
    return True

        cone_ok = all(is_trop_cone_numeric(m, d) for m in members)
        # total intersection is empty: the largest coordinate can never be beaten
        grid = [list(p) for p in product(range(-3, 4), repeat=d)]
        total = [x for x in grid if all(m(x) for m in members)]
        # every (d-1)-subfamily meets: the explicit witness of the proof
        all_small_meet = True
        for I in combinations(range(d), d - 1):
            k0 = next(k for k in range(d) if k not in I)
            witness = [0.0 if j == k0 else -1.0 for j in range(d)]
            if not all(members[k](witness) for k in I):
                all_small_meet = False
        print(f"\n  d = {d}:  family T_1..T_{d} of tropical cones")
        print(f"    all members are tropical cones (sampled):   {cone_ok}")
        print(f"    total intersection empty (grid search):     {len(total) == 0}")
        print(f"    every (d-1)-subfamily has a common point:   {all_small_meet}")
        print(f"    => Helly number is exactly d = {d}")

    print("\n  Helly FAILS for infinite families: C_k = {x in R^2 : x_0 + k <= x_1}.")

              f"{all(x[0] + k <= x[1] for k in range(N + 1))}")
    print("    but no x satisfies x_1 - x_0 >= k for every k in N.")

def cone_hull_point(P: Matrix, lam: Vector) -> Vector:
    """z_i = max_k (lam[k] + P[k][i])  -- a point of the tropical cone hull."""
    d = len(P[0])
    return [max(lam[k] + P[k][i] for k in range(len(P))) for i in range(d)]


def caratheodory_reduce(P: Matrix, lam: Vector) -> tuple[list[int], Vector]:
    """Select one generator per coordinate: at most d of them suffice."""
    z = cone_hull_point(P, lam)
    chosen: list[int] = []
    for i in range(len(z)):
        k_star = max(range(len(P)), key=lambda k: lam[k] + P[k][i])
        if k_star not in chosen:
            chosen.append(k_star)
    return sorted(chosen), z

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 5. Residuation and the principal solution
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def solve_maxplus(A: Matrix, b: Vector) -> tuple[bool, Vector, Vector]:
    """Decide A (x) x = b via the principal solution.  Returns
    (solvable, candidate A#b, residual A (x) (A#b))."""
    x_hat = resid(A, b)
    r = mul_vec(A, x_hat)
    return all(abs(r[i] - b[i]) < 1e-9 for i in range(len(b))), x_hat, r

        ([[0, 2], [3, 1]], [5, 10]),

    ]
    for A, b in tests:

        print(f"\n  A = {A},  b = {b}")
        print(f"    A # b (greatest subsolution) = {x_hat}")
        print(f"    A (x) (A # b)                = {r}")
        print(f"    solvable: {ok}" + ("" if ok else "   (best approximation from below)"))

    print("\n  Galois connection  A (x) x <= b  <=>  x <= A # b  (random check):")

def diff_feasible(d: int, cons: Sequence[tuple[int, int, float]]) -> bool:
    """Feasibility of  x[t] - x[s] <= w  by Bellman-Ford negative-cycle test."""
    dist = [0.0] * d
    for _ in range(d):
        for (s, t, w) in cons:
            if dist[s] + w < dist[t] - 1e-12:
                dist[t] = dist[s] + w
    return not any(dist[s] + w < dist[t] - 1e-12 for (s, t, w) in cons)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Max-plus arithmetic
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def trop_add(a: float, b: float) -> float:
    """Tropical addition a (+) b = max(a, b)."""
    return max(a, b)


def trop_mul(a: float, b: float) -> float:
    """Tropical multiplication a (x) b = a + b."""
    return a + b


def trop_det(M: Matrix) -> float:
    """Tropical determinant  max over permutations pi of  sum_r M[r][pi(r)].

    This is the value of the optimal assignment problem with cost matrix M.
    Brute force over m! permutations; fine for the small m used here.
    """
    m = len(M)
    if m == 0:
        return 0.0
    return max(sum(M[r][pi[r]] for r in range(m)) for pi in permutations(range(m)))


def mul_vec(A: Matrix, x: Vector) -> Vector:
    """Max-plus matrix-vector product  (A (x) x)_i = max_j (A[i][j] + x[j])."""
    return [max(A[i][j] + x[j] for j in range(len(x))) for i in range(len(A))]


def resid(A: Matrix, b: Vector) -> Vector:
    """Residuated vector  (A # b)_j = min_i (b[i] - A[i][j]).

    By the residuation theorem this is the greatest x with A (x) x <= b.
    """
    m, n = len(A), len(A[0])
    return [min(b[i] - A[i][j] for i in range(m)) for j in range(n)]


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Tropical Cramer dependence
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def delete_row(A: Matrix, k: int) -> Matrix:
    """The row-deleted minor A^(k-hat)."""
    return [row[:] for i, row in enumerate(A) if i != k]


def cramer_weights(A: Matrix) -> Vector:
    """Cramer weights lambda_k = tropdet(A with row k deleted).

    A is (d+1) x d.  By the tropical Cramer dependence theorem, for every
    column i the maximum of lambda_k + A[k][i] is attained at >= 2 rows.
    """
    return [trop_det(delete_row(A, k)) for k in range(len(A))]


def column_argmax_profile(A: Matrix, lam: Vector) -> list[tuple[float, int]]:
    """For each column: (value of the max, number of rows attaining it)."""
    out: list[tuple[float, int]] = []
    for i in range(len(A[0])):
        vals = [lam[k] + A[k][i] for k in range(len(A))]
        best = max(vals)
        out.append((best, sum(1 for v in vals if abs(v - best) < 1e-9)))
    return out


def is_tropically_dependent(A: Matrix, lam: Vector) -> bool:
    """Every column maximum of lambda_k + A[k][i] is attained at least twice."""
    return all(cnt >= 2 for _, cnt in column_argmax_profile(A, lam))

def helly_tight_set(k: int, d: int) -> Callable[[Vector], bool]:
    """Membership test for T_k = {x : exists j != k with x_k + 1 <= x_j}.

    Each T_k is a tropical cone; the family T_1..T_d has empty intersection but
    every d-1 of them meet.  This is the extremal family for Helly number d.
    """

    def member(x: Vector) -> bool:
        return any(j != k and x[k] + 1 <= x[j] + 1e-12 for j in range(d))

    return member


def is_trop_cone_numeric(member: Callable[[Vector], bool], d: int,
                         trials: int = 400) -> bool:
    """Monte-Carlo check that a set is closed under max-plus combinations."""
    import random

    for _ in range(trials):
        x = [float(random.randint(-5, 5)) for _ in range(d)]
        y = [float(random.randint(-5, 5)) for _ in range(d)]
        if not (member(x) and member(y)):
            continue
        s, t = float(random.randint(-4, 4)), float(random.randint(-4, 4))
        z = [max(s + x[i], t + y[i]) for i in range(d)]
        if not member(z):
            return False
    return True

        grid = [list(p) for p in product(range(-3, 4), repeat=d)]
        total = [x for x in grid if all(m(x) for m in members)]
        # every (d-1)-subfamily meets: the explicit witness of the proof
        all_small_meet = True
        for I in combinations(range(d), d - 1):

            witness = [0.0 if j == k0 else -1.0 for j in range(d)]
            if not all(members[k](witness) for k in I):
                all_small_meet = False
        print(f"\n  d = {d}:  family T_1..T_{d} of tropical cones")
        print(f"    all members are tropical cones (sampled):   {cone_ok}")

def cone_hull_point(P: Matrix, lam: Vector) -> Vector:
    """z_i = max_k (lam[k] + P[k][i])  -- a point of the tropical cone hull."""
    d = len(P[0])
    return [max(lam[k] + P[k][i] for k in range(len(P))) for i in range(d)]


def caratheodory_reduce(P: Matrix, lam: Vector) -> tuple[list[int], Vector]:
    """Select one generator per coordinate: at most d of them suffice."""
    z = cone_hull_point(P, lam)
    chosen: list[int] = []
    for i in range(len(z)):
        k_star = max(range(len(P)), key=lambda k: lam[k] + P[k][i])
        if k_star not in chosen:
            chosen.append(k_star)
    return sorted(chosen), z

    lam: Vector = [float(random.randint(-4, 4)) for _ in range(m)]
    G, z = caratheodory_reduce(P, lam)
    z_small = cone_hull_point([P[k] for k in G], [lam[k] for k in G])
    print(f"\n  {m} generators in R^{d}, point z = {z}")
    print(f"  reduced generator set G = {G}  (|G| = {len(G)} <= d = {d})")
    print(f"  z recomputed from G      = {z_small}   equal: {z == z_small}")

    print("\n  Sharpness: the d tropical unit vectors e^(k) "
          "(0 on the diagonal, -1 off).")

        zero = [0.0] * d
        full = cone_hull_point(E, [0.0] * d)
        # brute-force: can a proper subfamily generate 0?  Try residuated weights.
        proper_ok = False

                    proper_ok = True
        print(f"    d = {d}: full family generates 0: {full == zero}; "
              f"some proper subfamily does: {proper_ok}")

def solve_maxplus(A: Matrix, b: Vector) -> tuple[bool, Vector, Vector]:
    """Decide A (x) x = b via the principal solution.  Returns
    (solvable, candidate A#b, residual A (x) (A#b))."""
    x_hat = resid(A, b)
    r = mul_vec(A, x_hat)
    return all(abs(r[i] - b[i]) < 1e-9 for i in range(len(b))), x_hat, r

    { z : z_i = max_k (lam_k + p_k[i]) for some weights lam } .

are lam_k = min_i (z_i - p_k[i]), and z is in the hull if and only if these
weights reproduce z.  The script rasters the hull as ASCII art, and for every
point of the hull records how many generators the Caratheodory reduction keeps

Caratheodory theorem on three colour classes.

from __future__ import annotations

from collections import Counter

Matrix = list[list[float]]
Vector = list[float]

GENERATORS: Matrix = [
    [0.0, 0.0, 0.0],
    [0.0, 3.0, 1.0],
    [2.0, 0.0, 4.0],
    [4.0, 2.0, 0.0],
]


def residuated_weights(gens: Matrix, z: Vector) -> Vector:
    return [min(z[i] - g[i] for i in range(len(z))) for g in gens]


def combine(gens: Matrix, lam: Vector, d: int) -> Vector:
    return [max(lam[k] + gens[k][i] for k in range(len(gens))) for i in range(d)]


def in_hull(gens: Matrix, z: Vector, tol: float = 1e-9) -> bool:
    lam = residuated_weights(gens, z)
    w = combine(gens, lam, len(z))
    return all(abs(w[i] - z[i]) < tol for i in range(len(z)))


def caratheodory_reduce(gens: Matrix, z: Vector) -> list[int]:
    lam = residuated_weights(gens, z)
    chosen: list[int] = []
    for i in range(len(z)):
        k = max(range(len(gens)), key=lambda t: lam[t] + gens[t][i])
        if k not in chosen:
            chosen.append(k)
    return sorted(chosen)


def ascii_hull(gens: Matrix, lo: float = -3.0, hi: float = 6.0,
               cols: int = 74, rows: int = 30) -> str:
    marks = {}
    for k, g in enumerate(gens):
        x, y = g[0] - g[2], g[1] - g[2]
        cx = int(round((x - lo) / (hi - lo) * (cols - 1)))
        cy = int(round((y - lo) / (hi - lo) * (rows - 1)))
        marks[(cy, cx)] = str(k + 1)
    out_lines: list[str] = []
    for r in range(rows - 1, -1, -1):
        y = lo + r / (rows - 1) * (hi - lo)
        line = ""
        for c in range(cols):
            x = lo + c / (cols - 1) * (hi - lo)
            if (r, c) in marks:
                line += marks[(r, c)]
            else:
                line += "#" if in_hull(gens, [x, y, 0.0]) else "."
        out_lines.append(line)
    return "\n".join(out_lines)


def main() -> None:
    print(__doc__)
    print("Generators (in R^3, drawn in the chart):")
    for k, g in enumerate(GENERATORS):
        print(f"  p{k + 1} = {g}   chart point ({g[0] - g[2]}, {g[1] - g[2]})")
    print("\nTropical cone hull ('#' inside, digits mark the generators):\n")
    print(ascii_hull(GENERATORS))

    print("\nCaratheodory statistics over a grid of hull points:")
    counts: Counter[int] = Counter()
    for a in range(61):
        for b in range(61):
            z = [-3.0 + a * 0.15, -3.0 + b * 0.15, 0.0]
            if in_hull(GENERATORS, z):
                counts[len(caratheodory_reduce(GENERATORS, z))] += 1
    for size in sorted(counts):
        print(f"  {counts[size]:5d} hull points need exactly {size} generator(s)")
    print(f"  maximum needed: {max(counts)} (theoretical bound d = 3)")

    print("\nColourful Caratheodory check (3 colour classes, target z = 0):")
    z: Vector = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0]
    classes: list[Matrix] = [
        [[0.0, -2.0, -3.0], [-1.0, 0.0, -1.0], [-4.0, -1.0, 0.0]],
        [[0.0, -1.0, -2.0], [-3.0, 0.0, -4.0], [-1.0, -2.0, 0.0]],
        [[0.0, -3.0, -1.0], [-2.0, 0.0, -2.0], [-3.0, -3.0, 0.0]],
    ]
    for c, gens in enumerate(classes):
        lam = residuated_weights(gens, z)
        assert combine(gens, lam, 3) == z, f"z not in the hull of colour {c}"
    sel = []
    w: Vector = []
    for c, gens in enumerate(classes):
        lam = residuated_weights(gens, z)
        k = max(range(len(gens)), key=lambda t: lam[t] + gens[t][c])
        sel.append(gens[k])
        w.append(lam[k])
    rainbow = combine(sel, w, 3)
    print(f"  rainbow generators: {sel}")
    print(f"  weights           : {w}")
    print(f"  their combination : {rainbow}   equals z: {rainbow == z}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

<script>
const cv = document.getElementById('cv'), ctx = cv.getContext('2d');
const LO = -3.5, HI = 6.5;
let mode = 'gen';
let gens = [[0,0,0],[0,3,1],[2,0,4],[4,2,0]];
let query = null;

function toPix(x,y){
  return [ (x-LO)/(HI-LO)*cv.width, cv.height - (y-LO)/(HI-LO)*cv.height ];
}
function toMath(px,py){
  return [ LO + px/cv.width*(HI-LO), LO + (cv.height-py)/cv.height*(HI-LO) ];
}
function residWeights(u){
  return gens.map(g => Math.min(u[0]-g[0], u[1]-g[1], u[2]-g[2]));
}
function combine(idx, lam){
  const z=[-Infinity,-Infinity,-Infinity];
  idx.forEach((k,t)=>{ for(let i=0;i<3;i++) z[i]=Math.max(z[i], lam[t]+gens[k][i]); });
  return z;
}
function inHull(u){
  if(gens.length===0) return false;
  const lam = residWeights(u);
  const z = combine(gens.map((_,k)=>k), lam);
  return Math.abs(z[0]-u[0])<1e-9 && Math.abs(z[1]-u[1])<1e-9 && Math.abs(z[2]-u[2])<1e-9;
}
function caraSelect(u){
  const lam = residWeights(u), sel=[];
  for(let i=0;i<3;i++){
    let best=0;
    for(let k=1;k<gens.length;k++) if(lam[k]+gens[k][i] > lam[best]+gens[best][i]) best=k;
    if(!sel.includes(best)) sel.push(best);
  }
  return sel.sort((a,b)=>a-b);
}

function draw(){
  ctx.clearRect(0,0,cv.width,cv.height);
  // hull raster
  const step = 3;
  ctx.fillStyle = 'rgba(105,210,231,0.30)';
  if(gens.length>0){
    for(let px=0;px<cv.width;px+=step){
      for(let py=0;py<cv.height;py+=step){
        const [x,y] = toMath(px+step/2, py+step/2);
        if(inHull([x,y,0])) ctx.fillRect(px,py,step,step);
      }
    }
  }
  // grid
  ctx.strokeStyle='rgba(255,255,255,0.07)'; ctx.lineWidth=1;
  for(let v=Math.ceil(LO); v<=HI; v++){
    let p=toPix(v,LO); ctx.beginPath(); ctx.moveTo(p[0],0); ctx.lineTo(p[0],cv.height); ctx.stroke();
    p=toPix(LO,v); ctx.beginPath(); ctx.moveTo(0,p[1]); ctx.lineTo(cv.width,p[1]); ctx.stroke();
  }
  // axes
  ctx.strokeStyle='rgba(255,255,255,0.22)';
  let o=toPix(0,0);
  ctx.beginPath(); ctx.moveTo(0,o[1]); ctx.lineTo(cv.width,o[1]); ctx.stroke();
  ctx.beginPath(); ctx.moveTo(o[0],0); ctx.lineTo(o[0],cv.height); ctx.stroke();

  const sel = (query && inHull(query)) ? caraSelect(query) : [];
  if(query){
    const q=toPix(query[0]-query[2], query[1]-query[2]);
    sel.forEach(k=>{
      const g=gens[k], p=toPix(g[0]-g[2],g[1]-g[2]);
      ctx.strokeStyle='rgba(80,220,140,0.9)'; ctx.setLineDash([7,5]); ctx.lineWidth=2;
      ctx.beginPath(); ctx.moveTo(q[0],q[1]); ctx.lineTo(p[0],p[1]); ctx.stroke(); ctx.setLineDash([]);
    });
  }
  // generators
  gens.forEach((g,k)=>{
    const p=toPix(g[0]-g[2], g[1]-g[2]);
    ctx.fillStyle = sel.includes(k) ? '#7CFFB2' : '#ff6b6b';
    ctx.beginPath(); ctx.arc(p[0],p[1],7,0,6.2832); ctx.fill();
    ctx.fillStyle='#e8ecf8'; ctx.font='13px sans-serif';
    ctx.fillText('p'+(k+1), p[0]+10, p[1]-8);
  });
  // query
  if(query){
    const q=toPix(query[0]-query[2], query[1]-query[2]);
    ctx.fillStyle='#ffd166';
    ctx.beginPath();
    for(let i=0;i<10;i++){
      const r = i%2===0?11:4.6, a=-Math.PI/2 + i*Math.PI/5;
      const fn = i===0?'moveTo':'lineTo';
      ctx[fn](q[0]+r*Math.cos(a), q[1]+r*Math.sin(a));
    }
    ctx.closePath(); ctx.fill();
  }
  report(sel);
}

function fmt(v){ return (Math.round(v*100)/100).toFixed(2); }

function report(sel){
  const vd=document.getElementById('verdict'),
        tb=document.querySelector('#tbl tbody'),
        dt=document.getElementById('detail');
  tb.innerHTML=''; 
  if(!query){ vd.innerHTML='<span class="tag">place a query point</span>'; dt.textContent=''; return; }
  const lam=residWeights(query), inside=inHull(query);
  vd.innerHTML = inside
    ? '<span class="tag ok">query point IS in the tropical hull</span>'
    : '<span class="tag no">query point is NOT in the hull</span>';
  gens.forEach((g,k)=>{
    const tr=document.createElement('tr');
    tr.innerHTML = '<td>p'+(k+1)+' = ('+g.map(fmt).join(', ')+')</td><td>'+fmt(lam[k])+'</td><td>'+
      (sel.includes(k) ? '<b style="color:#7CFFB2">kept</b>' : (inside?'redundant':'—'))+'</td>';
    tb.appendChild(tr);
  });
  const z = combine(gens.map((_,k)=>k), lam);
  dt.innerHTML = 'query z = ('+query.map(fmt).join(', ')+')<br>'+
    'best max-plus approximation from below: ('+z.map(fmt).join(', ')+')'+
    (inside ? '<br>Carathéodory: '+sel.length+' of '+gens.length+
              ' generators suffice (bound: d = 3).'
            : '<br>The residuated candidate falls strictly short in some coordinate, so no weights work.');
}

cv.addEventListener('click', e=>{
  const r=cv.getBoundingClientRect();
  const px=(e.clientX-r.left)*cv.width/r.width, py=(e.clientY-r.top)*cv.height/r.height;
  const [x,y]=toMath(px,py);
  if(mode==='gen') gens.push([x,y,0]); else query=[x,y,0];
  draw();
});
document.getElementById('mode-gen').onclick=()=>{mode='gen';};
document.getElementById('mode-query').onclick=()=>{mode='query';};
document.getElementById('reset').onclick=()=>{gens=[[0,0,0],[0,3,1],[2,0,4],[4,2,0]];query=null;draw();};
document.getElementById('clear').onclick=()=>{gens=[];query=null;draw();};
draw();
</script>

*A guided tour of convex geometry in an arithmetic where addition is $\max$ and multiplication is $+$.*

---

## 1. A different arithmetic

Fix two operations on the real numbers:

$$a \oplus b = \max(a,b), \qquad a \odot b = a + b.$$

This is the **max-plus** (or **tropical**) semiring. It has no subtraction — you cannot undo a maximum — but it has everything else you need to do linear algebra: an associative, commutative "addition", a distributive "multiplication", and a rich supply of examples. Shortest paths, critical-path scheduling, dynamic programming, Viterbi decoding and the [tropicalisation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tropical_geometry) of algebraic varieties are all max-plus linear.

Once you have an arithmetic, you get a geometry. Replace the convex combination $\lambda x + (1-\lambda)y$ by

$$(s \odot x) \oplus (t \odot y) \;=\; \bigl(i \mapsto \max(s + x_i,\ t + y_i)\bigr),$$

and you get **tropical convexity**. A set closed under all such combinations (for arbitrary real $s,t$) is a **tropical cone**; a set closed under the normalised ones ($s=0$, $t \le 0$) is **tropically convex**.

<details>
<summary>Why two notions, and how do they differ?</summary>

Setting $y = x$ and $t = s$ in the cone definition shows that a tropical cone is invariant under **tropical scaling** $x \mapsto (s + x_1, \dots, s + x_d)$. So a tropical cone really lives on the *tropical projective torus* $\mathbb{R}^d/\mathbb{R}\mathbf 1$, one dimension down. A tropically convex set need not be scaling invariant. That single dimension is exactly what separates the two Helly numbers we will meet: $d$ for cones, $d+1$ for tropically convex sets.
</details>

---

## 2. See it first: the tropical polytope explorer

Before any theorem, get a feel for what these objects look like. Below, the tropical projective plane $\mathbb{R}^3/\mathbb{R}(1,1,1)$ is drawn in the chart $(u_1-u_3,\ u_2-u_3)$. The red dots are generators; the shaded region is their **tropical cone hull** — the tropical analogue of a polytope. Add generators, then place a query point and watch two theorems fire at once: an exact membership test, and a reduction of the generating set.

{{interactive_demo:0}}

Two things to notice while you play:

1. The hull is a union of **staircase** pieces, parallel to the coordinate directions and their diagonals. Tropical polytopes are contractible polyhedral complexes, never round.
2. However many generators you add, a point inside is always reproduced by **at most three** of them. That is the tropical Carathéodory theorem, and three is $d$ — the number of coordinates.

---

## 3. Membership by residuation: the Galois connection

How did the widget decide membership so fast? Suppose we want weights with $z_i = \max_k(\lambda_k + p_{ki})$. Any admissible weights must satisfy $\lambda_k + p_k \le z$ coordinatewise, and the **largest** weights with that property are

$$\lambda_k \;=\; \min_i\,\bigl(z_i - p_{ki}\bigr).$$

Since raising weights can only raise the combination, if any weights work then these do. One evaluation decides membership. This is a special case of the central optimisation tool of max-plus algebra.

> **Residuation Theorem.** For a matrix $A$, define $(A \otimes x)_i = \max_j (A_{ij} + x_j)$ and $(A\,\sharp\,b)_j = \min_i (b_i - A_{ij})$. Then for every $x$,
> $$A \otimes x \le b \iff x \le A\,\sharp\,b.$$
> In particular $A\,\sharp\,b$ is the greatest subsolution of $A \otimes x \le b$.

<details>
<summary>Click to reveal the two-line proof</summary>

($\Rightarrow$) For all $i,j$: $A_{ij} + x_j \le (A\otimes x)_i \le b_i$, so $x_j \le b_i - A_{ij}$; minimise over $i$.

($\Leftarrow$) For all $i,j$: $x_j \le (A\sharp b)_j \le b_i - A_{ij}$, so $A_{ij}+x_j \le b_i$; maximise over $j$. $\blacksquare$
</details>

And the payoff, due to Cuninghame-Green:

> **Principal Solution Criterion.** $A \otimes x = b$ is solvable **iff** the single canonical candidate $A\,\sharp\,b$ solves it. If $A\otimes x = b$ then $x \le A\sharp b$, so $b = A\otimes x \le A\otimes(A\sharp b) \le b$; the outer terms agree.

There is no elimination and no pivoting in max-plus linear algebra — just a closed formula and one check. Try it:

## 4. What replaces linear dependence?

Classically, $d+1$ vectors in $\mathbb{R}^d$ are linearly dependent: some nontrivial combination vanishes. Tropically there is nothing to cancel, so "vanishing" is replaced by a tie.

> **Definition.** Vectors $A_0,\dots,A_d \in \mathbb{R}^d$ are **tropically dependent** if there are weights $\lambda_k$ such that in every coordinate $i$ the maximum $\max_k(\lambda_k + A_{ki})$ is attained by at least **two** distinct indices.

> **Tropical Cramer Dependence Theorem.** Any $d+1$ vectors of $\mathbb{R}^d$ are tropically dependent. Explicit weights: $\lambda_k = \operatorname{tropdet} A^{(\hat k)}$, the **tropical determinant** $\operatorname{tropdet} M = \max_\pi \sum_r M_{r\pi(r)}$ of the matrix with row $k$ deleted.

The tropical determinant is precisely the value of an [optimal assignment problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assignment_problem): permanent and determinant coincide when there are no signs.

<details>
<summary>Click to reveal the full proof idea — "two equal columns" in max-plus</summary>

Fix a coordinate $i$ and prepend to $A$ a copy of its own $i$-th column, making a square matrix $\widetilde A$ with **two equal columns**.

*Laplace step.* For a permutation $\pi$ with $k = \pi^{-1}(0)$, deleting row $k$ and the prepended column shows $\sum_r \widetilde A_{r\pi(r)} \le \lambda_k + A_{ki}$, with equality for a good choice of $\pi$. Hence $\operatorname{tropdet}\widetilde A = \max_k(\lambda_k + A_{ki})$.

*Swap step.* Let $\pi$ be optimal and let $a, b$ be the rows receiving the two identical columns; $a \ne b$. Swapping their assignments changes nothing, because the two columns are equal, so the swapped permutation is optimal too.

*Conclusion.* The Laplace step applied to the two optimal permutations expresses the same optimum as $\lambda_a + A_{ai}$ and as $\lambda_b + A_{bi}$. Two maximisers. $\blacksquare$

Classically one swaps the equal *columns* and concludes the determinant is its own negative. Tropically, without signs, one swaps the two *rows carrying* them and concludes the optimum is not unique. **Non-uniqueness is the tropical form of vanishing.**
</details>

## 5. Helly's theorem, and the surprise

In 1913 Helly proved: if every $d+1$ members of a finite family of convex sets in $\mathbb{R}^d$ intersect, then all of them do. The number $d+1$ is optimal classically. Tropically it drops.

> **Tropical Helly Theorem.** Let $d \ge 1$ and let $C_1,\dots,C_n$ be tropical cones in $\mathbb{R}^d$. If every **$d$** of them have a common point, then all of them do.

The proof is where the tie earns its keep.

<details>
<summary>Click to reveal how dependence forces a common point</summary>

Induct on $n$. For each $k$, the induction hypothesis gives a point $y_k$ lying in every cone except possibly $C_k$. Take $d+1$ of these, let $\lambda$ be their Cramer weights, and form

$$z_i = \max_r (\lambda_r + y_{k_r, i}).$$

If $C_j$ is not one of the chosen indices, all the $y_{k_r}$ lie in it, so $z$ does too (cones are closed under max-plus combinations). If $C_j = C_{k_{r_0}}$, only the row $r_0$ is suspect — but the maximum in each coordinate is attained **twice**, hence by some row $r \ne r_0$, so the suspect row is redundant:

$$z_i = \max_{r \ne r_0} (\lambda_r + y_{k_r,i}).$$

Again $z \in C_j$. Since $j$ was arbitrary, $z$ lies in the whole intersection. $\blacksquare$
</details>

Is $d$ really optimal? Yes, and the extremal family is embarrassingly simple:

$$T_k \;=\; \{x \in \mathbb{R}^d : \exists\, j \ne k,\ x_k + 1 \le x_j\}\qquad (k=1,\dots,d),$$

"the $k$-th coordinate is beaten by another one". Any $d-1$ of them meet; all $d$ do not, because the largest coordinate of a point can never be beaten.

{{visualization:1}}

<details>
<summary>Why the tropical number is one smaller than the classical one</summary>

A tropical cone is scaling invariant, so it is determined by its image in the $(d-1)$-dimensional torus $\mathbb{R}^d/\mathbb{R}\mathbf 1$. Morally the classical count "$\dim + 1$" is being applied one dimension lower. The Cramer proof gets there without ever quotienting.

Drop scaling invariance and the unit comes back: for merely **tropically convex** sets the Helly number is exactly $d+1$, proved by homogenising $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$ to the scaling-invariant $\widehat S \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{d+1}$ and applying the cone theorem one dimension up. This settles a conjectured bound of $2d$ — true for all $d \ge 1$, but not sharp for $d \ge 2$ (and false in the degenerate case $d = 0$).
</details>

---

## 6. The loop closes: Helly *is* Cramer

Dependence gave us Helly. Remarkably, Helly gives back dependence. Assume the Helly property and take $d+1$ points $p_0,\dots,p_d$. Apply it to the $d+1$ "leave-one-out" hulls $H_k = \operatorname{tcone}\{p_j : j \ne k\}$; any $d$ of these share a point (the generator that the subfamily misses), so Helly yields $z \in \bigcap_k H_k$. Now residuate: $\lambda_j = \min_i(z_i - p_{ji})$. One checks $z_i = \max_{j \ne k}(\lambda_j + p_{ji})$ for every $k$ — precisely the "maximum attained twice" condition.

**So the tropical Helly theorem and the tropical Cramer dependence theorem are equivalent statements** — one geometric, one algebraic, two faces of the same tie.

---

## 7. Carathéodory: one generator per coordinate

> **Tropical Carathéodory Theorem (cones).** Every point of the tropical cone hull of a finite family in $\mathbb{R}^d$ lies in the hull of at most $d$ of the generators. The bound is sharp: the tropical unit vectors $e^{(k)}$ (with $0$ in coordinate $k$ and $-1$ elsewhere) generate $\mathbf 0$, which no proper subfamily generates.

The proof is a single sentence: for each coordinate keep one generator attaining the maximum there, and discard the rest; no coordinate loses its value and none can gain one.

{{visualization:0}}

There is even a **colourful** version, the tropical analogue of Bárány's theorem, and unlike the classical one it is completely explicit:

> **Colourful Tropical Carathéodory.** If a point $z$ lies in the tropical cone hull of each of $d$ colour classes in $\mathbb{R}^d$, then it lies in the hull of a rainbow selection — from class $c$, take a generator attaining the maximum in coordinate $c$.

{{algorithm:3}}

---

## 8. What it buys: certificates and schedules

A Helly theorem is really a statement about **certificates**: if a system has no solution, there is a small subsystem that already has none.

> **Locality of tropical feasibility.** A finite system of two-sided tropical inequalities $\max_j(a_{kj}+x_j) \le \max_j(b_{kj}+x_j)$ in $N$ unknowns is solvable iff every $N$ of the inequalities are.

> **Difference constraints.** A finite system $x_{t_k} - x_{s_k} \le w_k$ in $d$ variables is feasible iff every $d$ of the constraints are.

The second is a familiar face in disguise: difference constraints are shortest-path problems, feasible exactly when the associated digraph has no negative cycle — and a negative cycle can be taken simple, hence with at most $d$ arcs. The Helly bound $d$ and the [Bellman–Ford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellman%E2%80%93Ford_algorithm) criterion agree, because both express that max-plus dependence in $\mathbb{R}^d$ occurs already among $d$ objects.

{{algorithm:1}}

On the scheduling side, $A \otimes x = b$ asks whether a timetable can be met exactly; $A \sharp b$ is the latest admissible schedule, and the principal-solution criterion answers the question in $O(mn)$ time.

{{algorithm:2}}

<details>
<summary>Where the theory stops: infinite families</summary>

The cones $C_k = \{x \in \mathbb{R}^2 : x_1 + k \le x_2\}$, $k \in \mathbb{N}$, are tropical cones; every finite subfamily has a common point (take $x = (0, \max F)$), yet no point lies in all of them. Classically compactness repairs this. Tropical cones are never compact — they are invariant under the unbounded scaling action — so finiteness is genuinely essential, not a technical convenience.
</details>

## 10. Where next

Two questions sit right at the edge.

**Tropical Radon number.** Can any $d+1$ points of $\mathbb{R}^d$ be split into two nonempty groups whose tropical cone hulls intersect? A Radon partition is exactly a proper 2-colouring of the *argmax hypergraph* of a dependence witness (edge $M_i$ = the rows attaining the maximum in coordinate $i$): the split works iff every $M_i$ is bichromatic. The Cramer witness forces $|M_i| \ge 2$, but $d$ edges of size $\ge 2$ on $d+1$ vertices can still fail to be 2-colourable, so one must optimise over the *whole* dependence polytope rather than a single witness. Since that polytope is nonempty and explicitly constructed, the question is a concrete finite optimisation.

**Colourful tropical Helly.** Given $d$ colour classes of tropical cones in $\mathbb{R}^d$, if every rainbow selection has a common point, must some single class have one? The colourful Carathéodory theorem of §7 is exactly the ingredient such a proof would need.

Beyond that: fractional and $(p,q)$-type theorems with the constant $d$; the right compactness hypothesis on the projective torus to rescue infinite families; the symmetrised max-plus semiring, where "balanced" replaces "attained twice"; and the behaviour of all these constants when $-\infty$ entries are allowed.

Classical convexity counts dimensions. Tropical convexity counts coordinates. Change the arithmetic, and the geometry recounts.
